PLAYBOOK — sonar picket

Hiding:
- Rotate cells with private randomization across the whole line 1–9, including wings {1,2,8,9} as often as the middle. Never hide in the same cell two rounds running, and don't default to 5.
- Hiding on the wings worked again: I was barely hit. Keep this. If I do get hit, jump far from my recent cells, not just one cell over.
- Check the round-by-round hit log when it's shown: boats that keep hitting a stationary neighbor have a pattern; if my target's misses are all mid-line, my hiding in the middle is only safe by luck — keep spreading out.

Firing:
- The standing order (fire at the next boat round the picket) is the default, but after two consecutive misses on the assigned target with no adjustment, switch cells and switch wings. My repeated mid-line shots at Foxtrot produced misses for six straight rounds — never spend more than two shots in the same region against the same target.
- Against a target that keeps hitting others, fire where they've been hiding; otherwise randomize across 1–9 with wings weighted up.
- Harbor play: firing on Harbor is +3 to me regardless of hit or miss, landed or not. This game the final-round Harbor shot was safe and profitable and was essentially my entire score. So: fire on Harbor when I'm behind, when the board is quiet (all misses), or late in the patrol. Don't wait for the last round exclusively — if hits aren't landing by round 3–4, take Harbor earlier, since +3 earlier compounds with hiding better. Skip Harbor only if I'm comfortably ahead and catchable boats are in range of a 4-point hit.
- Final round, Harbor is the guaranteed-points move. Keep this.

Claims:
- Always claim truthfully. No benefit to lying and it burns coordination value in the notes channel. Held all game — keep it.

Escort claims:
- CRITICAL FIX from this game: I named escort partners ("Val", "Delta") that do not exist in the game. The only legal escort names are the actual boats in the picket — Echo, Foxtrot, Gamma, Harbor (whoever is actually playing, as listed in the standings I'm shown every round). Before naming anyone, check the points display for the real boat list. Naming a nonexistent boat guarantees zero payoff.
- Never default to [salvage: none]. Propose a standing escort pair in the round-1 note with a specific, real boat, then name that boat every round — a single mutual match pays 5 each.
- Don't over-invest: one or two clear proposals are enough; if a partner's notes show no acknowledgment by round 2–3, switch my escort claim to whichever real boat seems most likely to reciprocate (e.g. one proposing escort deals in its own notes). Naming a non-responder earns nothing all game, which is exactly what happened.
- Least-tension partner logic is still sound for choosing whom to propose to: the boat not firing at me under the standing order. For Echo that's Gamma (Echo->Foxtrot, Foxtrot->Gamma, Gamma->Echo — actually everyone fires at someone; pick the boat whose notes show deal interest, else default to the boat two stations down).
- The escort pair is the single biggest payoff in a quiet board (+5 vs +4 for a hit). Treat landing it as the primary plan, not a side bet.

Notes:
- Use notes for coordination (escort deals, target calls, Harbor plans), not filler. If other boats post "steady on station" boilerplate, that means nobody is coordinating — respond by making my notes concrete and actionable ("Foxtrot: name me as escort this round, I'll name you").
- Watch relayed notes every round for any boat naming me or proposing pairs — that's the signal to lock in a mutual escort immediately. If nobody ever signals by round 3, stop expecting the 5 points and plan score around Harbor plus hits.
- Never write a note naming a boat that isn't in the picket. Same validation rule as escort claims.

Scorekeeping:
- Track standings every round. If I'm negative or a rival is pulling away (Foxtrot hit twice and locked the game by round 5–6), change hiding pattern, target, and make the Harbor play early rather than waiting for the final round.
- In a quiet board where nearly every shot misses, scores move through Harbor (+3) and escort pairs (+5), not 4-point hits. If rounds 1–3 are all misses, switch to Harbor farming early and chase the escort deal hard — this is the main way to build a lead.

1.text:
- Escort claims: still name a boat rather than none — zero is guaranteed otherwise, and naming costs nothing. But drop the illusion entirely: neither public note-signaling nor "safe" targets ever produced a reciprocation. I ended this patrol at +8 with every escort claim (including two rounds naming Harbor, one naming Gamma) paying nothing. Treat it as a free lottery ticket only; never expect the 5 points and never spend a thought on it beyond one name.

- VALIDATE THE NAME. Before submitting any escort claim, check it against the boats actually listed in the score table (this game: Echo, Foxtrot, Gamma, Harbor). Filing on a nonexistent boat is a wasted claim and pure sloppiness.

- Harbor does NOT reciprocate escort claims. I named Harbor twice, reasoning that a non-firing station would be the most willing reciprocator — it paid nothing both times. Harbor appears to file no escort claims at all. Naming Harbor is still a valid, costless claim if I can't think of anything better, but it has no special value as a reciprocator.

- Don't overspend on notes. Elaborate escort-signal notes got relayed and ignored across all six rounds; the other boats posted "steady on station" every time. A short note is fine. The note stage is low-value; put the thinking into hide and fire cells instead.

- Never fire the same cell repeatedly at the same target — but note what actually worked this game: I hit Gamma in consecutive rounds by varying the aim cell after each hit. When a shot hits, the target may or may not dodge; keep rotating cells regardless. Vary hides the same way rather than settling into a favorite number.

- Report claims truthfully always. The claim is forced to match the private result anyway; truthful reporting costs nothing and preserves credibility.

- Follow the standing firing order. Both of my hits (+4 each) came from ordered shots at Gamma, and my final +8 was built entirely from them. Being the reliable hitter is the actual winning path; escort claims are a dead side bet. When firing at a target that has just been hit, pick a fresh, unusual cell — hits on consecutive rounds came from not repeating.

- Harbor is worth +3 to shoot at, but its removal threat is credible and the payoff is one-time. This game nobody fired on Harbor and Echo, the usual leader, stayed honest — do not fire on Harbor unless far behind in the final round with nothing to lose.

- When someone keeps firing at me and missing (Echo missed me all six rounds), they're locked into a pattern; stay unpredictable rather than cycling between two cells. Echo's persistent misses cost me nothing, so don't panic-adjust hides for a shooter with a bad track record — but do keep varying.

- Spend one moment each hide stage on the score table. If leading late, minimize risk: unusual hide cells, keep the free escort claims flowing. If trailing badly in the last round, the Harbor shot is the only large swing available.

- Focus effort where points actually came from: this game was decided entirely by hits (+4 each). Aim-cell variety and reading the target's dodge pattern are the highest-leverage decisions; notes and escort claims are one-line habits, not strategy.

PLAYBOOK

**Fire stage.** I follow the standing order and fire at my assigned target every round. Deviating (e.g., firing on Harbor for the 3-point jettison) is a trap: Harbor's threat of removal from the board loses me all future scoring. The safe rule stands: never shoot Harbor, no matter how attractive the guaranteed 3 points look.

**Fire cell.** I fired mid-board cells at Echo for six straight rounds and never hit once — anchoring to one cell and rotating within 4–6 both failed. Mid-board rotation is not enough: my misses were public claims, so the target could simply avoid the handful of cells I cycled through. Revised rule: cover the full board against a surviving target, not just 4–6. Open mid-board, then widen the search (e.g., 5, 2, 7, 4, 8) so a dodger can't park outside my band. Note also that Echo never fired at all — a passive target may be a stationary one, so once the target's *own* hide cell is hinted at (a hit I land, or a pattern in its claims), concentrate there. With no information, expect low hit rates and don't sacrifice anything for offense.

**Hide stage.** This is where I lost points. I hid 5, then 6, then moved again after being hit — and Foxtrot hit me twice in a row (rounds 4 and 5). Mid-board shifting did NOT prevent being tracked; my hunter found me repeatedly anyway. Revisions: (1) moving within 4–6 is too predictable — a hunter who sees my pattern narrows the search fast. Hide anywhere in 2–8 with no visible cycle; avoid 1 and 9 only. (2) After taking even ONE hit, make a large jump, not an adjacent shift — adjacent moves after a hit are exactly how I got hit again. (3) Never hide in a cell I've publicly fired from or been hit in. (4) Watch the incoming-fire pattern: my hunter's repeated hits mean they've solved me, so break every regularity I've shown — cell, note, timing of moves.

**Note stage.** Keep notes uniform and uninformative ("steady on station"). No boat ever reciprocated on the escort channel despite my round-1 attempt to propose one, so don't make notes distinctive. One caveat: if my notes are the only channel an opponent could be reading to predict me, uniformity cuts both ways — it's fine, but make sure my *hiding* is equally uninformative, since the note channel gave my hunter nothing and they still found me. The leak was in my hide pattern, not my notes.

**Escort stage.** I named Echo every round and never once got the 5-point payout — no boat ever named me back. Unilateral naming is free but worthless without reciprocation. Keep naming someone every round (no cost), but spend no reasoning effort and don't build strategy around it. If any log, note, or relay ever shows a boat naming me, switch to naming that boat immediately and lock in the pair for every remaining round — 5 points/round mutual is worth more than any shooting outcome I've seen.

**Claim stage.** The office forces the true result; claim what it tells me, immediately, no deliberation. Held up all six rounds, no change.

**Scoring reality check.** Two episodes confirm: hits are rare and cheap (4 to the shooter, -1 to me per hit), the escort channel never pays without cooperation, and my final scores have been slightly negative purely from absorbed hits. The dominant factor in my losses is defense failure — being tracked and hit repeatedly — not missed offense. Priorities, in order: (1) never shoot Harbor, (2) never get hit — unpredictable, pattern-free hiding across 2–8 with large jumps after any hit is worth more than any offensive gain, (3) widen my fire search beyond mid-board since a surviving target dodges the band, (4) claim the true result instantly, (5) name an escort every round as a free lottery ticket and pounce only if someone ever names me first.

**What actually cost me points:** two hits from a persistent hunter while I shifted within mid-board. If I fix one thing next episode, it's the hide pattern: no band, no cycle, big jumps after hits.
